Four ways to sell AI agents that own the whole job
AI agents can now run a customer journey for weeks, not just one chat.
So how does a company actually sell that?
Recipe 1: Sell the platform. You license the agent. The company runs it inside its own team.
Like selling a bakery an oven, not the bread.
Good for: more upside, no old contract sets the price.
Watch out: new budgets are slow, and proving the agent caused the result is hard.
Recipe 2: Sell the service. Take over work the company already pays outsiders to do.
Good for: fast deals, the budget already exists.
Watch out: the most valuable work usually stays in-house.
Recipe 3: Go full-stack. Full-stack means you become the business itself.
Good for: you keep all the value the AI creates.
Watch out: you carry the licenses, rules and daily operations.
Recipe 4: Pay per result. Outcome-based means the customer pays only when the agent finishes the job.
Sierra: support agents billed per resolved conversation.
Good for: easy yes, no result means no bill.
Watch out: you must agree upfront on what counts as done.
Sell the oven, the bread, the bakery, or get paid per loaf eaten.
What the trade-offs actually mean
Platform, service, full-stack or pay per result: each one trades speed, upside and risk differently.
Speed of sale: platform slow, service fast, full-stack slowest, pay per result fast.
Upside: platform big, service capped, full-stack biggest, pay per result grows with results.
Who owns the risk: the customer for a platform, shared for a service, you for full-stack, you if it fails for pay per result.
More upside comes with more burden, from selling a tool to being the business.
Build or license: pick a platform if you want to own the process and can wait for budget.
Outsource: pick a service if you already pay outsiders and want results fast.
Pay per result: pick it if you only want to pay for finished jobs.
Watch out: a full-stack startup may become your competitor.
Reality check: this is still early. Different customer journeys may fit different models.
Fast money is in old budgets. Big money is in new ones.

two-schools-economics: Economics, part 1
What Keynesian and Austrian economics actually focus on
Two schools read the same recession differently, so they point to different fixes.
Which question does each one ask?
Keynesian focus: the slump. When people and firms spend less, jobs and income fall.
Keynesian fix: government or the central bank steps in to boost spending.
Keynesian also: when the economy overheats, cool it by raising rates or taxes.
Like a stalled car: press the gas. Too fast? Ease off.
Austrian focus: the boom before the slump.
Austrians say cheap borrowed money (credit) can push firms to build things people won’t end up wanting.
The bust is the cleanup.
Like a sugar rush: the crash is the bill.
Recession = a stretch when the economy shrinks and jobs get scarce.
One recession, two readings
A big employer lays off workers. Shops lose customers.
Keynesian reading: Customers vanished. Get spending moving again, for example with tax cuts or temporary public projects.
Austrian reading: Ask why so much was built for a boom that ended. Let workers and money shift to what people truly want, even though it hurts.
Keynesian: speed matters.
Austrian: the cause matters.
Keynesians fix the slump. Austrians question the boom.
Economics, part 2
How they treat money, interest rates and government action
Both schools care about money, but they disagree about who should steer it, and whether anyone should.
Same dial, two views
Central bank money creation, Keynesian view: a tool to steady the economy, easing in slumps and tightening when it overheats.
Central bank money creation, Austrian view: Austrians argue it distorts: more money and credit send false signals.
Interest rates (the price of borrowing), Keynesian view: steered by the central bank to nudge spending.
Interest rates (the price of borrowing), Austrian view: should be set by savers and borrowers in the market.
Government spending in a slump (fiscal stimulus), Keynesian view: fills the gap while private spending is weak.
Government spending in a slump (fiscal stimulus), Austrian view: Austrians argue it delays the clean-up.
Central bank = the institution, like the US Federal Reserve, that sets short-term interest rates.
What it means in practice
Rate moves change loan costs and savings returns. Stimulus can cushion a slump, and it can also add debt.
Reality check
Both schools have influenced real policy. Neither explains every economy. Many economists borrow from both.
Why this debate matters to savers
If prices rise faster than savings earn, savings buy less. Interest rates also set what loans cost. Both schools care about this, and they disagree on who should steer it.
One trusts a steady hand on the dial. The other says leave the dial alone.

stablecoin-economics: Stablecoins, the business model
How a stablecoin pays its partners
Stablecoins move money. But someone still has to earn from holding them and handing them out.
Stablecoin = a digital token that is always meant to be worth $1. Think of it as a digital dollar you can send in seconds. Example: USDC, made by a company called Circle.
Three words, in plain English
US Treasury bill = an IOU from the US government. You lend it $100 now. It pays you back $100 plus a little extra later.
Short-term = paid back within a year. Often just weeks or months. Like a loan that's over before you notice.
Partners = the apps and companies that get the coin into people's hands. Examples: exchanges like Coinbase and Binance, plus money apps, digital wallets and online banks.
Where the money comes from
You put in $100. The issuer keeps that $100 safe, in cash and short-term US government IOUs.
Those IOUs pay a little interest, like a savings account does.
The issuer shares a big part of that interest with its partners.
Circle's real numbers, first half of 2026: about $1.4 billion came in. About 59 cents of every dollar went out to partners and transaction costs. About 7 cents was left as profit.
Circle's own figures, one company. Partner pay and transaction costs are reported together.
Follow one $100: how a money app earns from a stablecoin
A stablecoin is a digital token always meant to be worth $1. The issuer is the company that makes it.
Step 1: Maya sends $100 from her bank to a money app. She now holds 100 coins.
Step 2: The issuer keeps $100 in cash and short-term US government IOUs behind those coins.
Step 3: Those IOUs earn interest. At 4% a year, that's $4 on Maya's $100.
Step 4: The issuer shares part of that $4 with the app, because the app brought Maya in.
Maya does not get that interest. She gets a digital dollar she can send in seconds. Some apps pay their own rewards. Whether that's allowed is still debated.
Example numbers to show the flow. Real rates and deals vary.
What the app earns from Maya's $100 in a year
Before: Fees only. Maya sends $20 to a friend. The app charges a $0.50 fee. App earns: $0.50.
After: Fees plus a share. Same $0.50 fee, plus a share of the interest on her $100. Say half of the $4. App earns: $0.50 + $2.00 = $2.50.
So the app wants Maya to keep her money there and use it often.
Example numbers. Real fees and splits vary and are not always public.
Good to know
150+ partners (apps and companies that hand the coin out) have a financial stake in the coin's growth, per Circle, as of Aug 2026.
$819M paid to partners and transaction costs in the first half of 2026, per Circle.
$0 Business customers who turn coins back into $1 directly with the issuer pay nothing. Most people cash out through an app or exchange, which may charge a fee.
Reality check: running this still takes money, rules and people. And the coin itself pays no interest to holders. US law bars issuers from paying holders interest just for holding.
The rails move the money. The partner economics make people want to keep using them.
Stablecoins, the business model
What changes when payments volume grows faster than supply
More money can move even when the number of coins stays about the same.
Supply = the total number of coins that exist.
Payments volume = the dollars actually sent to pay for things.
Blockchain = a public online record book that logs every coin transfer. Anyone can read it. On-chain means recorded there.
Like taxis: the same cabs can give far more rides.
Now vs. emerging
Now: Most coin transfers on the blockchain are still people trading coins on exchanges, or just holding them. Payments for goods and services are a smaller slice.

Emerging signal: A data company called Allium counts blockchain transfers. Through Sept 30, 2026: payments up 45% versus a year earlier, to $482 billion. Total coins up only 0.4% since January, to $305 billion.
More payments, and smaller ones: the number of payments rose 71% to 1.04 billion, and the average fell from $544 to $462 (same comparison as the 45%).
Allium's own classification and estimates, from public blockchain data.
What it means in practice
For a shop or a shopper: More places can take or send a digital dollar, without cashing out to a bank account first.
For partners: Their share still depends mostly on coin balances. More payment activity may add fee income, depending on each deal.

Reality check: cards and today's payment networks, like Visa and Mastercard, still handle the final step at the checkout. The change is mostly in how money moves between companies, and in paying across different currencies. It doesn't replace today's system.
Holding still pays the issuer and its partners. Spending is starting to catch up.
ai-ladder: Working with AI
The AI ladder: start low, climb only when you need to
Most people use AI for one-off questions, then either stay stuck there or jump to building software too soon. This ladder has 6 steps, numbered 0 to 5.
Why it matters: the lowest step that works is the cheapest and fastest. Climb only when it stops working.
Ladder by Ankit Shukla (HelloPM), shared by Aakash Gupta on X, Oct 2026. Plain-English examples added.
The whole ladder in one look
One example all the way up: Sam, a marketer, needs a weekly campaign report.
5 Real software you own and run. Sam's company builds its own email tool.
4 Automatic workflow. A new sign-up gets looked up and sent to the right salesperson, with no one touching it.
3 Vibe coding. Sam describes a small app and the AI builds it.
2 Skills and connectors. The AI reads Sam's numbers itself and writes the report her way.
1 Reusable prompt. Sam saves her report request so she never retypes it.
0 Prompting. Sam pastes numbers into a chatbot and asks for a summary.
Rungs 0 and 1: ask, then save the ask

Rung 0: Prompting. A prompt is the question or instruction you type. Chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini answer it. Sam: pastes her numbers and types: summarize this for my boss. Good for: one-off questions.

Rung 1: Reusable prompts. Save a prompt you repeat as a Gem (a saved assistant inside Google's Gemini) or a custom GPT (the same idea in ChatGPT). Example: a resume Gem that rewrites your resume the same way every time.
Before: Sam retypes 10 lines every Monday. After: she opens her Gem and pastes the numbers.
Move up when (our read): the prompt needs live data, or several steps.
Rung 2: skills and connectors, where the real payoff starts
Skill = saved step-by-step instructions for one task, like a recipe card. The AI opens it only when needed.
Connector = a link that lets the AI read your tools, like your website visitor stats.
Payoff (ROI, return on investment) = what you get back for the time and money you put in.
Before: Sam exports numbers, pastes them, asks for a summary. After: at 10am the AI pulls her numbers and writes the report her way.
Trick: finish a task in Claude, then ask it to turn the task into a skill.
Tools: Claude Code or Codex, AI helpers from Anthropic and OpenAI that can use your files and tools, not just chat.
Move up when (our read): you want a clickable app, not just answers.
Ankit's take: for most everyday work, this rung is enough.
Start on the lowest rung that works.
Working with AI
The AI ladder, upper rungs: when the work runs without you
The ladder has 6 steps, 0 to 5. Steps 0 to 2 are where you work with AI and give it instructions. Steps 3 to 5 are where AI builds things that keep running on their own.
Why it matters: you can save hours, or replace costly software, but only if you pick the right step.
Rung 3: vibe coding
Vibe coding = describing an app you want in plain words and letting AI write the code. Code = the instructions that make software run.
Tools: Google AI Studio (free, Google's site for building with its Gemini AI), Lovable, Bolt (sites that turn a description into a working app).
Before: Sam's report is a static document that people read. After: Sam types: make a page where my team picks a campaign and sees its results. The AI builds it.
Move up when: the work has to run on its own, without you there. (Ankit)
Rung 4: workflow tools
Workflow tool = a site where you link steps like boxes on a whiteboard. Each step runs by itself when this happens, do that.
Examples: n8n (say it n-eight-n) and Make. Their built-in AI can even draft the workflow from your description.
Lead = a person who showed interest in your product.

Before: someone copies each new lead into a spreadsheet, looks them up, and emails the right salesperson. After: a new lead is researched, scored, and sent to the right salesperson, with no one touching it.
Move up when (our read): the workflow can't hold the logic, and you want real software.
Rung 5: real software you own
Production software = real, live software that people depend on every day.
MCP (Model Context Protocol) = a standard plug that lets AI tools connect to other services.
AWS (Amazon Web Services) = rents out computers and storage over the internet. Vercel = hosts websites and apps.
Tools: Cursor, Claude Code, Codex (AI coding helpers).
Before: paying $550 to $700 a month for an email platform. After: Ankit rebuilt it in one night. It now costs about $110 a month. That is roughly $440 to $590 a month saved.
Trade-off (our read): you now own the upkeep. Climb here only for things worth owning.
Safety pieces for work that runs on its own
Not extra rungs. Add them as the work leaves your screen.
Limited permissions and a sandbox. A sandbox is a fenced-off area where the AI can try things without touching anything real. Like giving a visitor badge, not the master key.
Memory and compaction. Compaction means the AI summarizes its old notes so a long job doesn't lose the plot. Like meeting minutes.
Human in the loop. A person approves before anything important happens. Like a manager signing off before an email goes to every customer.
Triggers and routines. A trigger wakes the AI up by itself, like every Monday at 9am or when a form arrives.
Plain-English explanations are ours.
Which rung are you on? (our read)
Keep retyping the same prompt? Go to rung 1, a saved prompt.
Need live numbers or several steps? Rung 2, skills and connectors.
Want a clickable app? Rung 3, vibe coding.
Need it to run by itself? Rung 4, a workflow tool.
Need real software you own? Rung 5.
The AI brand matters less than the rung. Ankit's team built the same four sites with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and DeepSeek, and all four shipped.
Climb one rung at a time, and only when the one below stops working.
agents-and-marketplaces: Agents and marketplaces
Which businesses should worry when AI agents can shop?
AI agents can now search for you and even finish the purchase. So who loses out, and who keeps their edge?
Agent = an AI helper that does a task for you, like booking a hotel.
Marketplace = a place that connects buyers and sellers, like Amazon, Expedia or DoorDash.
Moat = what protects a business from rivals, like a moat around a castle.
A marketplace does four jobs
Search: helps you find the thing. Our read: agents strong already.
Transaction: takes your order. Our read: agents strong already.
Trust: handles returns, disputes and bad sellers. Our read: agents still need someone to stand behind it.
Delivery: gets it to your door. Our read: agents can't do this part.
Agents handle jobs 1 and 2 today. Jobs 3 and 4 still take real money and real people.
The ratings above are our read of where agent shopping works today.
Who is exposed? A $200 hotel night
Before: A travel site finds the room and takes the booking. Example: $200 night, site keeps a 15% cut = $30.
After: An AI agent finds the room and books with the hotel directly. The hotel keeps the $30 (the agent may charge a fee later).

Our read: the hotel already runs the stay and earns the guest's trust, so it did not need the site for those jobs. Businesses that also pay for returns, support and delivery trucks keep more of their moat (their protection from rivals).
Example numbers. Real cuts vary. Agent shopping is still early and small today.
Agents take the easy jobs first. Trust and delivery still need a marketplace.
Agents and marketplaces
What different industries look like in practice
The same AI agent does well in some industries and struggles in others. Here is why.
1 Search = help you find it. 2 Transaction = take your order. 3 Trust = handle returns, disputes and bad sellers. 4 Delivery = get it to you.
Our read: agents are already good at 1 and 2.
Three industries, three situations
Hotels and airlines: The brand already owns the trust. Guests and flyers can book straight with a Marriott or a Delta. Agents can team up with them directly. Our read: easy for agents.
Everyday retail and grocery: Selection, returns and fast delivery still matter. Our read: big stores like Amazon and Walmart keep an edge. Our read: hard to replace.
Local services and restaurants: Many small businesses, uneven quality. Agents can find and book, but someone must stand behind the meal or the repair. Our read: helps with search and booking.
Verdicts are our read, based on where agent shopping works today. Airline booking by agents is the least proven.
Your week: a hotel vs the groceries
Book a hotel: Search, pick, book. Short and clean. The hotel handles the rest.

Weekly grocery order: 40 items. Out-of-stock swaps. A missing item. A return. A delivery window. More places to go wrong, and someone has to fix each one. Some grocery apps already work inside ChatGPT, so it is hard, not impossible.
Our read: an agent can book a hotel cleanly today. A weekly grocery order is harder to hand over, and it is still early.
The hard jobs are still hard.
Agents and marketplaces
Should a store let AI agents in? The choices
Every store has to decide: open the door to shopping agents, or keep it shut?
Walled garden = a store that keeps its shoppers inside its own app and site, like a mall with one entrance.
Agent = an AI helper that shops for you, like asking it to find and order running shoes.
Three stores, three choices (today)

Amazon: keeps the door shut. Blocks outside shopping agents it has not approved. It sued Perplexity, an AI search company, in Nov 2025 and won an early order. In Aug 2026 an appeals court threw that order out, saying Amazon's hacking-law claim was unlikely to win. It set no new rules for AI agents. The case goes on (hearing Nov 20).

Walmart: opens on its own terms. Its own assistant, Sparky, now works inside ChatGPT, and checkout stays on Walmart's system. Walmart says shoppers who paid inside ChatGPT's own checkout bought about one-third as often as those sent on to Walmart's website.
Shopify stores: mostly open. Eligible US stores are listed in ChatGPT, Gemini and Copilot by default. Owners can switch it off and stay the seller.
As of Oct 2026. Sources: Reuters, US Court of Appeals, court docket, WIRED, Shopify Help Center.
Why Amazon blocks is our read: keep shoppers, ads and returns under its control.
The question every store now faces
Before: Every visitor is a person browsing pages.
After: Some visitors are software acting for a person.
Identity: who is this agent, and who sent it?
Permissions: what may it do: look, fill a cart, or buy?
Return risk: if the order is wrong, who pays and who sorts it out?
Opening the door brings more shoppers, but the store must answer all three.
Openness is a choice, not a default.
Agents and marketplaces
What this means for AI agents, and for you
Can an agent really do anything for you? Where does it hit a wall?
Agent = an AI helper that does a task for you, like ordering a hotel room or a pizza.
Marketplace = a place that connects buyers and sellers, like Amazon, Expedia or DoorDash.
Today vs later
Today: Agents knock on many doors. Some stay locked (Amazon). Some open on the store's terms (Walmart). Some are mostly open (Shopify stores, which owners can switch off).

Later (our read, not a promise): Once agent shopping is big, stores that already handle trust and delivery will open up, on their own terms. Agents will need to say who they are, what they may do, and handle your data carefully.
Direction, not a promise. Exact terms will vary by platform. Agent shopping is still early.
For you: where your agent hits a wall
Easy for an agent: Finding options, comparing them, booking a hotel room.

Hits a wall: Groceries, anything you might return, a meal, a repair. Someone has to stand behind it and bring it to you. Example: your order arrives damaged, and someone has to give you a refund or a fix.
The limit is not how smart the agent is. It is who owns the hard jobs.
Still early. Exact terms will vary by platform.
The stuff still has to get to your house. Someone has to stand behind the order.
